title: The Hellenistic & Parthian Gulf
subtitle: c.300 BC–300 AD · Tylos, Mleiha and Gerrha — Greek Coins, Caravan Wealth and the India Route

categories.label: Power
categories.subtitle: Seleucid Tylos, the Abiel coin-kings of the Oman peninsula, and Characene overlordship

entries.label: Seleucid administration of Tylos and the Erythraean islands
entries.hint: After Alexander, Bahrain became 'Tylos', an island under Seleucid oversight. A Greek inscription names a 'governor of Tylos and Dilmun', and the towns took Greek forms — the Gulf's brief Hellenistic moment.
entries.note: Greek inscription of the Seleucid period from Bahrain naming an official over Tylos and Dilmun (Gatier, Lombard & Al-Sindi, 2002); Strabo 16.3.4 on Tylos and Arados.

entries.label: The Abiel coinage — rulers of the lower Gulf
entries.hint: Silver coins struck at Mleiha copy Alexander tetradrachms but carry the Aramaic name 'Abiel', sometimes 'Abiel daughter of...' — the name of a ruler or dynasty of the Oman peninsula kingdom the Greeks called Omana. Whether Abiel was a queen, a king or a house is still debated.
entries.note: D.T. Potts, 'The Pre-Islamic Coinage of Eastern Arabia' (1991) and 'Supplement' (2002); the 'Abiel' legends on the Mleiha/ed-Dur series.

entries.label: Mleiha — fort, palace and royal necropolis
entries.hint: Mleiha was the inland capital: a mud-brick fort with corner towers, a large columned building, a mint, iron workshops and a cemetery of monumental tower-tombs with camel and horse burials. It is the seat of the Abiel power.
entries.note: French and Belgian missions at Mleiha (Boucharlat; Mouton; Sharjah Archaeology Authority); M. Mouton, 'La péninsule d'Oman de la fin de l'âge du Fer au début de la période sasanide' (2008).

entries.label: Characene draws Tylos into its orbit
entries.loc: Spasinou Charax (head of the Gulf); Tylos
entries.hint: Hyspaosines founded the kingdom of Characene at the head of the Gulf, and its kings came to dominate Tylos and the sea lanes. Characene coins circulate throughout the Gulf; a Characene satrap of Tylos is attested.
entries.note: Characene coinage and the satrap-of-Tylos evidence (Potts 1990, vol. 2); Pliny NH 6.147 on Characene; Isidore of Charax.

entries.label: Ardashir I ends the Parthian Gulf order
entries.hint: The Persian historian al-Tabari records that Ardashir I, founder of the Sasanian Empire, campaigned in eastern Arabia and killed the king of Bahrain, named as Sanatruq. Mleiha was abandoned within a generation; the Gulf passed under Sasanian control.
entries.note: al-Tabari, 'History' I.820 (Bosworth trans.), on Ardashir's Arabian campaign and the killing of the king of al-Bahrayn; the terminal date of Mleiha (Mouton 2008). Bridges to the Sasanian Gulf folio.

categories.label: Conflict
categories.subtitle: Antiochus at Gerrha, the burning of Mleiha and the Sasanian campaign

entries.label: Antiochus III's expedition against Gerrha
entries.hint: Returning from the east, Antiochus III sailed against the caravan city of Gerrha. Its people met him with an embassy and a vast payment — 500 talents of silver, a thousand talents of frankincense — and he sailed away, leaving them their independence and their trade.
entries.note: Polybius 13.9. The location of Gerrha (Thaj? al-Uqayr? Hofuf?) remains debated.

entries.label: Contest for the head of the Gulf
entries.hint: Characene's control of the Gulf's most valuable choke-point made it a recurring target for the Parthian kings and, briefly, for Trajan's Rome (116 AD). The instability at the Gulf head shaped who could trade down its length.
entries.note: Cassius Dio 68.28–29 (Trajan at Charax, 116 AD); the Parthian–Characene relationship (Schuol, 'Die Charakene', 2000).

entries.label: The destruction and abandonment of Mleiha
entries.hint: Mleiha's fort shows a burning and rebuilding in the 2nd century, then final abandonment in the 3rd. The end of the Abiel kingdom coincides with the rise of the Sasanians and a shift of activity to the coast.
entries.note: Mleiha fort stratigraphy (Mouton; Sharjah Archaeology Authority); the correlation with Ardashir's campaign is likely but not proven.

entries.label: Ardashir's Arabian campaign
entries.hint: Ardashir I's move into eastern Arabia — attested by al-Tabari and echoed in later tradition — brought the whole Gulf under a single imperial power for the first time since the Achaemenids and closed the Parthian-era world of independent coin-kings.
entries.note: al-Tabari I.820; Sasanian expansion into the Gulf discussed in the Sasanian Gulf folio and in Potts (1990) vol. 2.

categories.label: Order
categories.subtitle: Greek governors, local mints and the epigraphic habit

entries.label: A governor 'of Tylos and the islands'
entries.hint: A Greek dedication from Bahrain records an official responsible for Tylos and the neighbouring islands — evidence that the Seleucids ran the Gulf as a defined administrative district, with Greek as its language of government.
entries.note: Gatier, Lombard & Al-Sindi, 'Greek inscriptions from Bahrain', Arabian Archaeology and Epigraphy 13 (2002).

entries.label: Local minting at Mleiha
entries.hint: The Oman peninsula kingdom struck its own silver — first close copies of Alexander types, then increasingly local designs and legends. Issuing coinage was a claim to sovereignty as much as a convenience for trade.
entries.note: Potts, 'The Pre-Islamic Coinage of Eastern Arabia' (1991); die studies of the Mleiha mint.

entries.label: Hasaitic funerary inscriptions and their formulae
entries.hint: Dozens of tombstones in the eastern Arabian 'Hasaitic' script name the deceased, their lineage and a protective deity, sometimes with a curse on anyone who disturbs the grave. They are the region's own legal-religious response to the Hellenistic epigraphic habit.
entries.note: A. Sima, 'Die hasaitischen Inschriften' (Nebes, ed., 1999); Hasaitic corpus from Thaj and the al-Hasa oasis.

entries.label: Characene coinage as a Gulf-wide currency
entries.loc: Charax; circulating to Bahrain, ed-Dur, Mleiha
entries.hint: The tetradrachms and drachms of the Characene kings turn up in hoards and site finds the length of the Gulf. Whoever controlled Charax effectively set the coinage that Gulf merchants used.
entries.note: Characene coins in Gulf hoards (ed-Dur, Bahrain); Schuol, 'Die Charakene' (2000).

categories.label: Belief
categories.subtitle: The sun-god of ed-Dur, Greek dedications on Tylos and the animal burials

entries.label: The temple of Shams at ed-Dur
entries.hint: A small square temple at ed-Dur, with altars and a well, was dedicated to Shams, the sun deity, named in an Aramaic inscription on the site. It is the best-preserved pre-Islamic temple in the UAE.
entries.note: Belgian mission at ed-Dur (Haerinck); the Aramaic 'Shams' inscription; E. Haerinck, 'The temple at ed-Dur' (in the ed-Dur series).

entries.label: Greek cult on Tylos
entries.hint: Hellenistic Bahrain has yielded Greek votive inscriptions, including a dedication to the Dioscuri, and figurines in Greek style. Greek religion arrived with the garrison and the traders and coexisted with older Gulf cults.
entries.note: Gatier, Lombard & Al-Sindi (2002); Hellenistic terracottas from Bahrain (Bahrain National Museum).

entries.label: Camel and horse burials at Mleiha and ed-Dur
entries.hint: Elite tombs at Mleiha were accompanied by the burials of camels, and sometimes horses, often with harness and saddlery. The rite ties the warrior aristocracy of the Abiel kingdom to their mounts in death.
entries.note: Mleiha animal burials (Mouton; Jasim, 'The Necropolis of Mleiha', 1999); ed-Dur camel graves.

entries.label: Aramaic and the goddess of the eastern Arabian tombs
entries.hint: Hasaitic tomb texts invoke a small pantheon — chiefly a goddess whose name is written 'at' — to protect the dead. Eastern Arabia kept its own religion while writing it in a script and idiom shaped by contact with the Aramaic and South Arabian worlds.
entries.note: Sima, 'Die hasaitischen Inschriften' (1999); the divine name and its possible link to Athtar / Allat.

categories.label: Expression
categories.subtitle: Tower tombs, imported glass and the gold mask of Thaj

entries.label: The tower tombs of Mleiha
entries.hint: Mleiha's dead of rank were buried under square mud-brick towers, some plastered and multi-storeyed, standing above ground as visible monuments. They revive, in a new form, the peninsula's old habit of monumental burial.
entries.note: S. Jasim, 'The Necropolis of Mleiha' (Sharjah, 1999); Mouton (2008).

entries.label: The Thaj gold funerary set
entries.loc: Thaj, eastern Saudi Arabia (grave of a young woman)
entries.hint: A child or young woman at Thaj was buried with a gold face-mask, a gold-mesh glove, pearl-and-gold earrings, a necklace of gold and rubies and a girdle. It is the richest pre-Islamic burial known from eastern Arabia and shows the wealth Gerrhaean-era trade concentrated there.
entries.note: The 'Thaj treasure', excavated 1998; published by the Saudi Commission for Tourism and National Heritage; exhibited in 'Roads of Arabia'.

entries.label: Imported luxury at ed-Dur
entries.hint: ed-Dur produced Roman cast and mould-blown glass, a Roman bronze figurine, Rhodian and Mesopotamian amphorae, Parthian glazed jars and Indian pottery — a coastal town furnished from every shore of the Indian Ocean and Mediterranean.
entries.note: ed-Dur excavation series (Belgian mission; Danish; French); the ed-Dur glass corpus (Whitehouse); Roman bronze head of a youth.

entries.label: The Abiel coins as portraiture
entries.hint: Over generations the Herakles head on the Mleiha coins drifts away from its Greek model into a distinctive local style — stylised curls, large eye, added symbols. The series is a small case study in an imported art form being made one's own.
entries.note: Potts, 'The Pre-Islamic Coinage of Eastern Arabia' (1991), on the stylistic devolution of the Abiel series.

categories.label: Thought
categories.subtitle: Writing returns in three scripts, and the Greeks map the Gulf

entries.label: Androsthenes of Thasos surveys the Gulf for Alexander
entries.loc: Gulf coast from Charax to Tylos
entries.hint: Alexander sent three captains to explore the Arabian shore; Androsthenes sailed furthest and wrote a lost 'Voyage along the Indian Coast' describing Tylos, its pearls and its 'wool-bearing trees'. It is the first scientific account of the Gulf.
entries.note: Androsthenes cited by Theophrastus (HP 4.7) and Strabo (16.3); Arrian, 'Indica' 43 and 'Anabasis' 7.20 on Alexander's Gulf reconnaissance.

entries.label: Cotton on Tylos — Theophrastus's 'wool-bearing trees'
entries.hint: Theophrastus, drawing on Androsthenes, describes trees on Tylos that bear wool — cotton, grown and spun on Bahrain around 300 BC. It is among the earliest records of cotton cultivation west of India.
entries.note: Theophrastus, 'Historia Plantarum' 4.7.7–8; discussed by Bowen, 'Ancient trade routes in the Persian Gulf' and Potts (1990).

entries.label: A trilingual epigraphic culture
entries.hint: Eastern Arabia in this period writes in Greek (Bahrain), Aramaic (ed-Dur, coins), and the local Hasaitic script (tombstones) — sometimes on the same sites. After a millennium of near-silence, the region is literate again, in several traditions at once.
entries.note: Greek: Gatier et al. (2002); Aramaic: the ed-Dur and coin legends; Hasaitic: Sima (1999).

categories.label: Economy
categories.subtitle: Gerrha's incense, Tylos pearls and the port the Periplus called Omana

entries.label: Gerrha, 'the richest of all tribes'
entries.hint: Strabo and Pliny describe Gerrha as fabulously wealthy on the incense trade: south Arabian frankincense and myrrh came overland to Gerrha and were shipped up the Gulf, or sent by caravan to Petra and the Mediterranean. Its people, they say, built with blocks of salt.
entries.note: Strabo 16.3.3; Pliny NH 6.147–150; Agatharchides. The Thaj–Gerrha identification is favoured by many but unproven.

entries.label: Omana — the Gulf's port on the India run
entries.hint: The 'Periplus of the Erythraean Sea' names Omana as a Gulf port trading directly with the Indian coast — sending out pearls, purple, dates, wine and slaves, taking in copper, teak, sandalwood and ebony. ed-Dur is its likeliest site.
entries.note: 'Periplus Maris Erythraei' §36 (Casson ed., 1989); the Omana = ed-Dur identification (Potts; Salles).

entries.label: The pearls of Tylos
entries.hint: Greek and Roman writers single out Tylos for its pearls — Isidore of Charax, Pliny and others describe the fishery and the trade. The Gulf's oldest industry was now a name-brand luxury in the Roman Mediterranean.
entries.note: Isidore of Charax, 'Parthian Stations'; Pliny NH 9.106; Athenaeus 3.93. Bahrain's Hellenistic pearl trade.

entries.label: Mleiha, the Gulf's iron town
entries.hint: Mleiha held the largest concentration of iron-smelting furnaces yet found in south-east Arabia, turning out tools and weapons. The Abiel kingdom's wealth rested on manufacturing as well as on transit trade.
entries.note: Mleiha metallurgical area (Mouton; Sharjah Archaeology Authority); iron production scale discussed by Ploquin & the French mission.

entries.label: Characene and the Charax–India axis
entries.loc: Spasinou Charax, head of the Gulf
entries.hint: Charax, at the mouth of the Tigris, was where goods from India and the Gulf met the caravan roads to Palmyra and the Parthian interior. Its kings grew rich as gatekeepers, and their coinage financed the whole Gulf trade.
entries.note: Isidore of Charax; the Palmyrene trade inscriptions naming Charax; Schuol, 'Die Charakene' (2000).

categories.label: Technology
categories.subtitle: Iron furnaces, mud-brick fortification and monsoon sailing

entries.label: Iron smelting at scale
entries.hint: Batteries of small shaft furnaces at Mleiha, with their slag heaps and ore stores, represent the peninsula's first large iron industry — the technology that armed the Abiel aristocracy and equipped its trade.
entries.note: Mleiha iron-working area, French mission reports; comparative scale noted by Mouton (2008).

entries.label: The mud-brick fort of Mleiha
entries.hint: A square enclosure with projecting corner towers and a central courtyard building, rebuilt after a burning — Mleiha's fort is the peninsula's first true fortification since the Bronze Age towers, adapted to a world of cavalry and iron weapons.
entries.note: Mleiha fort excavation (Boucharlat; Mouton; Sharjah Archaeology Authority).

entries.label: Monsoon sailing on the Gulf–India route
entries.loc: Gulf of Oman and Arabian Sea
entries.hint: By the 1st century AD, Gulf shippers were using the seasonal monsoon winds to run directly to and from the Indian coast, as the Periplus describes for Omana. Larger sewn-plank vessels made the open-water crossing routine.
entries.note: 'Periplus Maris Erythraei' on the sailing seasons; the debate over the 'discovery' of the monsoon (Hippalus) — Casson (1989).

categories.label: Exchange
categories.subtitle: Palmyrenes at Charax, Roman glass at ed-Dur, and the two roads to India

entries.label: The Gulf as Rome's back door to India
entries.hint: When Red Sea routes were taxed or blocked, Indian goods flowed instead up the Gulf: from the Indian coast to Omana, on to Charax, and overland to Palmyra and the Mediterranean. The Gulf was the alternative artery of the Rome–India trade.
entries.note: 'Periplus' §36; the Palmyrene caravan inscriptions; Young, 'Rome's Eastern Trade' (2001).

entries.label: Palmyrene merchants at Spasinou Charax
entries.hint: Palmyra's trade inscriptions repeatedly honour citizens who led caravans to Charax or served as 'satrap of Tylos' for the Characene king. A resident Palmyrene community linked the Syrian desert city to the Gulf.
entries.note: Palmyrene tariff and honorific inscriptions (e.g. the caravan texts of the 130s AD); a Palmyrene as 'satrap of Tylos' under Meredates of Characene. Cross-references the Palmyrene Empire folio.

entries.label: Roman and Parthian goods on the Arabian shore
entries.hint: Roman glass and bronzes, Parthian glazed pottery, Rhodian wine amphorae and Indian ceramics arrive together at ed-Dur. The lower Gulf coast consumed the products of every surrounding civilisation and re-exported many of them.
entries.note: ed-Dur imports (Belgian and Danish missions); Haerinck, 'Excavations at ed-Dur' volumes.

entries.label: Indians and Characenes at ed-Dur
entries.hint: Indian cooking pots, a possible Brahmi graffito and quantities of Characene coin at ed-Dur suggest resident foreign traders — Indian and Mesopotamian — living in the port alongside its Arabian population.
entries.note: Indian Red Polished Ware and coarse wares at ed-Dur; the site's coin profile (heavily Characene). Haerinck, ed-Dur series.

entries.label: Gerrha's caravans to Petra and the Mediterranean
entries.hint: Overland caravans carried Gerrhaean goods across the peninsula to the Nabataean network and the ports of the Levant. Eastern Arabia's incense wealth and Nabataean Petra's were two ends of the same road.
entries.note: Strabo 16.4.4 on the Gerrha–Nabataea caravan route; cross-references the Nabataean Kingdom folio.

categories.label: World
categories.subtitle: Alexander's unfinished Arabian plan, the rise of Characene and the Sasanian turn

entries.label: Alexander's Arabian project
entries.hint: Alexander planned to circumnavigate Arabia and settle colonies on Tylos and on Icarus (Failaka), sending survey ships ahead. His death in Babylon left the scheme unexecuted — but Greek names and settlers reached the Gulf anyway.
entries.note: Arrian, 'Anabasis' 7.19–20; the Failaka ('Ikaros') Greek sanctuary and stele (Hellenistic garrison).

entries.label: Characene emerges as an independent Gulf kingdom
entries.hint: As Seleucid power collapsed, Hyspaosines carved out the kingdom of Characene at the Gulf head. For the next 350 years an independent, coin-minting state controlled the point where the Gulf trade met Mesopotamia.
entries.note: Characene foundation c.127 BC (Schuol 2000); Hyspaosines' coinage.

entries.label: Rome and Parthia fight over the trade roads
entries.hint: The long Roman–Parthian contest over Armenia and Mesopotamia repeatedly disrupted the overland routes, pushing traffic onto the Gulf and making Characene and Palmyra alternately rich and vulnerable.
entries.note: Cassius Dio and Tacitus on the Roman–Parthian wars; the effect on eastern trade (Young 2001).

entries.label: The Sasanians replace the Parthians
entries.hint: Ardashir I's overthrow of the Parthian Arsacids brought a centralising dynasty to Iran that took direct interest in the Gulf. Within two decades the age of independent Gulf coin-kings was over.
entries.note: Battle of Hormozdgan (224 AD); Ardashir's subsequent Gulf and Arabian campaigns (al-Tabari). Cross-references the Sasanian folios.

categories.label: Lives
categories.subtitle: The gold-mask girl of Thaj, women in the tomb inscriptions, and the ambiguous name Abiel

entries.label: The gold-mask burial of Thaj
entries.hint: The richest pre-Islamic grave in eastern Arabia belongs to a girl or young woman, buried with a gold face-mask and a fortune in gold, pearls and rubies. Whatever her personal status, her family channelled enormous wealth into a female burial.
entries.note: The Thaj treasure (Saudi excavations, 1998); the individual is identified as a young female.

entries.label: Women as tomb-owners in the Hasaitic texts
entries.hint: Hasaitic tombstones sometimes name a woman as the person for whom the tomb was made, and frequently trace descent through the mother. Eastern Arabian commemoration gave women a visible place in the record.
entries.note: Sima, 'Die hasaitischen Inschriften' (1999); the frequency of matronymics in the corpus.

entries.label: Was Abiel a queen?
entries.hint: Some Mleiha coins read 'Abiel daughter of...', a matronymic formula unusual for a male ruler. Scholars are divided on whether Abiel was a reigning queen, a dynastic founder-figure, or simply a house name — a reminder of how thin the ground is here.
entries.note: Potts (1991; 2002) reviews the readings; the 'daughter of' formula and its interpretation remain open.
